1.summary: Paul thanks God for Philemon's love and faith, then appeals to him, out of love rather than command, to receive back Onesimus, whom Paul calls his own heart, as a beloved brother; he offers to repay anything owed and is confident Philemon will do even more.
1.lookfor: Notice how carefully Paul makes his request, the pun on Onesimus's name, and the shift from slave to brother.

names.name: Philemon
names.gloss: A believer in Colossae who hosted a house church and owned Onesimus.

names.name: Apphia
names.gloss: A sister in the faith, probably Philemon's wife.

names.name: Archippus
names.gloss: A fellow soldier of Paul, perhaps Philemon's son.

names.name: Onesimus
names.gloss: Philemon's slave, converted through Paul in prison.

names.name: Epaphras
names.gloss: The founder of the Colossian church, now Paul's fellow prisoner.

insights.title: A house church
insights.body: The letter is to Philemon and the church in your house (1:2). Early believers met in homes; Philemon's household would hear how he responded, which put gentle pressure on him.

insights.title: Appeal, not command
insights.body: Though Paul could command him, for love's sake he appeals instead (1:8-9). Paul wants Philemon's goodness to be voluntary, not forced (1:14).

insights.title: Useful
insights.body: Onesimus means useful. Paul writes that he was once useless to Philemon but now is useful to both of them (1:11). A wordplay with a serious point: grace changed him.

insights.title: A runaway slave
insights.body: A runaway slave in Roman law could be beaten, branded or even killed. Paul sends Onesimus back with this letter as protection, calling him my very heart (1:12).

insights.title: More than a slave
insights.body: Receive him no longer as a slave, but more than a slave, a beloved brother (1:16). Paul doesn't attack slavery head-on, but the gospel makes master and slave brothers, and that truth eventually undermined slavery itself.

insights.title: Charge it to me
insights.body: If he has wronged you or owes you anything, put that on my account; I will repay it (1:18-19). Many readers see a picture of Christ, who takes our debt on himself.

insights.title: Even more
insights.body: Paul is confident Philemon will do even more than he asks (1:21), perhaps freeing Onesimus. A bishop of Ephesus named Onesimus around AD 110 may have been the same man.

insights.title: Welcoming back
insights.body: Philemon was asked to welcome someone who had wronged him, as a brother. Is there someone you need to receive back in that way?

intro.who: Paul, with Timothy (1:1), writing from prison to Philemon, a believer in Colossae, and the church that met in his house. Almost all scholars accept it as Paul's.
intro.when: About AD 60–62, carried by Onesimus along with the letter to the Colossians.
intro.why: Onesimus, Philemon's slave, had run away or left under a cloud, met Paul in prison and become a believer. Paul sends him back, asking Philemon to welcome him no longer as a slave but as a beloved brother, and offering to pay any debt himself.

outline.title: Greeting, thanks, and the appeal for Onesimus
